paper_title: Learning Where to Split: Dynamic Band Splitting for Audio Source Separation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Audio source separation models must preserve fine spectral structure while keeping the cost of the separator tractable. Band-split architectures reduce this cost by manually partitioning the spectrum into predefined frequency bands and encoding each band as a token, but the same boundaries are used for every mixture. Because informative spectral structure varies with source content, fixed boundaries can merge discriminative components or spend tokens where little resolution is needed. We introduce Dynamic Band Splitting (DBS), an end-to-end framework that adapts boundary locations and band widths to each mixture under a fixed band-token budget. DBS predicts content-conditioned boundary scores within frequency blocks, selects a prescribed number of boundaries using hard Top-$K$, and applies content-dependent pooling to obtain compact band tokens. After separation, it smooths and expands these tokens to the original STFT grid, refines them along frequency, and decodes complex masks with a frequency-shared head. DBS improved separation over the corresponding static models on DnR v2, MUSDB18-HQ, and EchoSet, with DBS-BSRNN achieving relative gain of 29.0% in average SI-SDR on DnR v2. These results and boundary analyses on DnR v2 show that content-adaptive frequency partitioning benefits multiple separator backbones under a fixed band-token budget. Code and audio demos are available at https://cslikai.cn/Dynamic-Band-Splitting

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Audio source separation aims to recover individual sources, such as speech, musical instruments, and environmental sounds, from recorded mixture. It supports music remixing and audio restoration (Rafii et al., 2018; Stoter et al., 2019; Li et al., 2026), hearing assistance (Li et al., 2025), and meeting transcription and automatic subtitle generation (Raj et al., 2021). These applications require representations that capture source-specific acoustic structure across heterogeneous mixtures. Source separation methods encode mixture into acoustic features, model dependencies within these features, and reconstruct the constituent sources. Representative methods include convolutional models such as Conv-TasNet (Luo & Mesgarani, 2019), encoderdecoder networks such as Demucs (Defossez et al., 2019), and attention-guided models such as TDANet (Li et al., 2023). Alongside advances in separator design, band splitting compresses the spectral features supplied to the separator. BSRNN (Luo & Yu, 2023) first represents the mixture as complex spectrogram using the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), then uses manually specified non-uniform layout to group its frequency bins into bands and map each band to fixed-dimensional representation before modeling temporal and inter-band dependencies. Subsequent architectures, including BS-RoFormer (Lu et al., 2024), Mel-Band RoFormer (Wang et al., 2023a), and TIGER (Xu et al., 2025), also construct Bingzhe Zhang and Kai Li contribute equally to the article. Corresponding authors. 1 Figure 1: DBS partitions across 30-second Tears of Steel excerpt. Each column represents non-overlapping three-second window, showing its midpoint frame, dominant acoustic content, and predicted partition. Colored lines highlight five learned boundaries per block; faint lines show the others, and black lines mark fixed block limits. compact band representations using predefined frequency layouts. This reduces the frequency-axis sequence from individual STFT bins to smaller set of bands, lowering the cost of subsequent separation. However, these band-split methods apply the same frequency layout to every mixture (Luo & Yu, 2023; Lu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). Their allocation of frequency resolution is therefore determined in advance, even though the locations and density of informative spectral components vary with the sources present. wide band may compress several discriminative components into single representation, while finely divided bands elsewhere may cover less informative content. Increasing the number of bands provides finer resolution but also increases the computational cost of the separator. The resulting challenge is to adapt the allocation of frequency resolution to each mixture while keeping the number of band representations fixed. We propose Dynamic Band Splitting (DBS), an end-to-end framework that learns mixture-dependent frequency partitions under fixed band-token budget. DBS divides the spectrograms frequency axis into fixed frequency blocks and predicts content-dependent boundary scores within each block. Hard Top-K selection forms prescribed number of contiguous bands per block, allowing their locations and widths to change across mixtures. After separation, the band features are smoothed in token order and expanded to the original STFT grid for full-resolution reconstruction. This design decouples the frequency resolution used by the separator from that of its output and supports integration with different backbones, including BSRNN (Luo & Yu, 2023) and TIGER (Xu et al., 2025). Figure 1 illustrates this behavior on continuous 30-second movie excerpt: the block scaffold and 128-band budget remained fixed, while the learned boundaries changed with the acoustic content. We evaluated DBS on the DnR v2 benchmark for music, speech, and sound-effect separation (Petermann et al., 2022), MUSDB18-HQ for music separation (Rafii et al., 2019), and EchoSet for speech separation (Xu et al., 2025). Relative to the BSRNN result, DBS-BSRNN improved average SISDR on DnR v2 by 29.0%. DBS-BSRNN improved four-stem SDR over the static BSRNN model on MUSDB18-HQ by 6.8% and improved the reported BSRNN SDRi on EchoSet by 3.6%. The gains extended to other band-split backbones: BS-RoFormer (Lu et al., 2024) and MelRoFormer (Wang et al., 2023a) outperformed their static counterparts in four-stem SDR on MUSDB18-HQ, while DBS-TIGER exceeded the TIGER SDRi on EchoSet. Boundary analyses and fixed-boundary controls on DnR v2 showed that DBS adapted its partitions to the input and improved separation under fixed band-token budget.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Band-Split-Based Audio Source Separation. Timefrequency-domain source separation methods such as Open-Unmix (Stoter et al., 2019) and TF-GridNet (Wang et al., 2023b) make spectral structure explicit, but processing high-resolution spectrograms over the full frequency axis can be computationally expensive. Band-split-based source separation methods address this cost by dividing the spectrum into subbands and assigning specialized modules to model within-band structure and cross-band interactions. Band-Split RNN (BSRNN) (Luo & Yu, 2023), BS-RoFormer (Lu et al., 2024), Mel-Band RoFormer (Wang et al., 2023a), and TIGER (Xu et al., 2025) instantiate this design with different subband representations and cross-band modeling modules. SCNet (Tong et al., 2024) integrates subband-specific compression into hierarchical encoderdecoder, coupling frequency downsampling with corresponding upsampling stages and skip connections. Across these designs, the frequency layout is treated as model-level structural prior: boundaries and band widths are specified by design and shared across inputs. Adaptive Spectral Representation and Frequency Allocation. Learnable filterbanks and inputconditioned modules relax the fixed spectral front end in different ways. Multi-Channel Masking with Learnable Filterbank (Dai et al., 2023) optimizes the spectral front end during training, whereas Spectral Feature Compression (SFC) (Saijo & Bando, 2026) replaces the fixed band-split encoder with shared sequence-modeling module based on cross-attention or Mamba. Sparsely gated mixture-of-experts source separation models (Wang et al., 2022) have been used to balance separation quality, speech distortion, and computational cost, while TF-MoE (Hu et al., 2026) routes experts along the time and frequency axes. These methods adapt the spectral representation or computational path within particular separation model. DBS instead learns input-dependent boundaries between contiguous frequency bands while keeping the number of bands fixed. Its boundary predictor is optimized jointly with the separator, and the original STFT grid is retained for reconstruction.

sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Datasets. We evaluated DBS on DnR v2 (Petermann et al., 2022), MUSDB18-HQ (Rafii et al., 2019), and EchoSet (Xu et al., 2025), covering cinematic, music, and speech source separation. DnR v2 contains music, speech, and sound effects; MUSDB18-HQ provides vocals, drums, bass, and other stems; and EchoSet contains two-speaker mixtures with noise and reverberation. At the sample rates used here, DnR v2 and MUSDB18-HQ had 022.05 kHz analyzed frequency range, whereas EchoSet had 08 kHz range. This contrast let us examine adaptive band allocation across different spectral bandwidths. Dataset construction and split sizes are detailed in Appendix E. Compared systems. On DnR v2, we trained fixed-band and DBS variants of BSRNN and TIGER from scratch, each with 128 bands. Appendix F.1 details how each backbones original partition was expanded to 128 bands. On MUSDB18-HQ, we trained fixed-band and DBS variants of BSRNN, BS-RoFormer, and MelRoFormer as single models that jointly estimated all four stems. This differed from the target-specific models used by the original BSRNN and BS-RoFormer systems (Luo & Yu, 2023; Lu et al., 2024). All MUSDB models used only the MUSDB18-HQ training split, without external audio, and were implemented in the Music-Source-Separation-Training framework.1 On EchoSet, we compared DBS-BSRNN and DBS-TIGER with the systems reported by TIGER (Xu et al., 2025). Appendix F.2 details the backbone substitutions. Training and evaluation. DBS used four frequency blocks and fixed band-token budget. DnR v2 and MUSDB18-HQ used 1025 STFT bins and 128 band tokens, whereas EchoSet used 321 bins and 67 band tokens. Each inference window determined one partition shared by band encoding and fullresolution reconstruction. We reported source-wise SI-SDR and its unweighted average on DnR v2, four-stem SDR on MUSDB18-HQ, and SDRi and SI-SDRi on EchoSet. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced Dynamic Band Splitting (DBS), which adapts frequency boundaries to each mixture under fixed band-token budget. DBS-BSRNN improved separation on DnR v2, and DBS variants improved the evaluated band-split backbones on MUSDB18-HQ and EchoSet. On DnR v2, matched boundary substitution and fixed-boundary training controls showed that boundary placement affected separation quality. Block and component ablations further identified the roles of per-block budgets, boundary scoring, and frequency refinement. These results show that allocating fixed frequency-resolution budget according to the mixture can improve separation without lengthening the separators token sequence. Limitations. DBS kept the number of bands fixed and selected one partition per inference window, so it did not adapt representation size or boundary positions within window. Preliminary learnablecount variants tended to select the largest admissible per-block budget, suggesting that variablebudget routing requires an explicit complexity constraint.

sections.content: Table 6 summarizes the sampling rates, recording durations, and training/test partitions of the three benchmarks. DnR v2. Divide and Remaster (DnR v2) (Petermann et al., 2022) provides synthetic monaural soundtracks for separating music, speech, and sound effects.3 Music clips were drawn from FMA, speech from LibriSpeech, and sound effects from FSD50K. The construction procedure varied source overlap and relative loudness to approximate soundtrack mixing, with foreground events and background ambience combined into the sound-effects stem. Each mixture and its three reference stems were released as 60-second waveforms at 44.1 kHz. The official v2 release contains 3,406 training, 487 validation, and 973 test mixtures. We used the complete training and test partitions Its combination of music, speech, and heteroand evaluated all 973 full-length test recordings. geneous environmental events provides diverse spectral content for studying input-dependent band allocation. MUSDB18-HQ. MUSDB18-HQ (Rafii et al., 2019) is the uncompressed version of MUSDB18 and contains 150 full-length stereo songs spanning multiple genres.4 Each track is provided at 44.1 kHz as mixture and four isolated stems: vocals, drums, bass, and other, with other collecting the remaining accompaniment. The recordings originate primarily from DSD100 and MedleyDB, together with additional contributed tracks. The uncompressed WAV release retains audio bandwidth 2TIGERs public small-model configuration, commit 9f18d4a: https://github.com/ JusperLee/TIGER/blob/9f18d4a10a7137e1ce8052cfb62215179f1287b6/configs/ tiger-small.yml. The large-model configuration uses the same losses. 3Dataset download: https://zenodo.org/records/6949108. 4Dataset download: https://zenodo.org/records/3338373. 15 up to approximately 22 kHz, beyond the approximately 16 kHz bandwidth of the AAC-compressed version. We used the official partition of 100 training tracks and 50 test tracks, without external training audio. Each model was trained to estimate all four stems jointly, and evaluation used the complete test tracks. EchoSet. EchoSet (Xu et al., 2025) targets two-speaker separation with noise, reverberation, and variable temporal overlap.5 LibriSpeech utterances were rendered with SoundSpaces 2.0 in Matterport3D indoor scenes, accounting for room geometry, object occlusion, and acoustic material properties. The two speakers occupied the same room, with sourcemicrophone distances sampled between 1 and 5 m. Their speech signals were combined at randomly sampled overlap ratios and mixed with background noise from WHAM!. The official splits contain 20,268 training, 4,604 validation, and 2,650 test mixtures, each six seconds long at 16 kHz. We used the released training partition and evaluated all 2,650 complete test mixtures. Both targets are speech, and the 16 kHz sampling rate gives an analyzed frequency range of 08 kHz, complementing the broader-bandwidth DnR v2 and MUSDB18-HQ benchmarks. SNR instead compares the estimate with the reference at its original amplitude scale: SNR(u, v) = 10 log10 v2 2 v2 2 . sections.content: Table 9 reports separation quality on EchoSet. Relative to the published BSRNN scores, DBSBSRNN improved SDRi by 0.46 dB and SI-SDRi by 0.43 dB. DBS-TIGER exceeded the published TIGER scores by 0.33 and 0.31 dB on the same metrics, respectively. Improvements with both backbones showed that the DBS interface also benefited speech separation within EchoSets 0 8 kHz analyzed range. INFERENCE-TIME BOUNDARY SUBSTITUTION We replaced the predicted boundaries of the trained DBS-BSRNN model on DnR v2 with uniform or BSRNN-layout boundaries while keeping model weights, input windows, and the 128-band budget fixed. The learned partition improved average SI-SDR by 1.27 and 0.45 dB over these fixed partitions, respectively  (Table 10)  . Within the trained model, boundary placement alone therefore affected separation quality.

The learned waveform filters had no ordering constraint; 80 adjacent filter indices had peak frequencies that reversed by more than 1 kHz.
